Structure–Residual Inductive Biases
for Language Model Pretraining

Hai Huang    Bartosz Żuk Affiliation: Palona AI  Institute of Computer Science, Polish Academy of Sciences    Rassul Magauin Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence    Jiaxin Huang Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence    Xue Liu Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Abstract

Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure–residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure–residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual

1 Introduction

The dominant recipe for improving language models is remarkably simple: scale the model, the data, and the compute, and optimize next-token prediction (NTP) (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Under this paradigm, the training process—primarily gradient-based optimization—is trusted not only to learn the predictive task, but also to discover how the information required for that task should be internally represented.

We ask a different question: should representation structure itself be an inductive bias?

A principled starting point is the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity. An object can be described by first specifying a structure ZZ, and then specifying the residual information required to recover the particular realization XX:

𝖪⁡(X)≤𝖪⁡(Z)+𝖪⁡(X∣Z)+O⁡(1).\mathsf{K}(X)\leq\mathsf{K}(Z)+\mathsf{K}(X\mid Z)+O(1).

This suggests a general inductive principle for language models: encourage internal representations to discover a favorable balance between structure and residual.

What should such structure look like in a language model? We draw inspiration from two basic functions involved in language modeling.

First, perception often involves abstraction. Phrases such as “France’s capital” and “the capital of France” differ at the token level but share substantial predictive structure. This suggests compressing information that must be carried across spans into a compact representation. However, a structure-only representation is insufficient: the exact surface realization still matters for autoregressive prediction. Motivated by this structure–residual balance, we introduce Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC), which routes information from a completed segment to later segments through a boundary carrier while preserving ordinary token-level autoregression within the current segment (Figure 1(a)). Related approaches include MEGABYTE’s combination of global patch modeling and local autoregressive byte decoding (Yu et al., 2023a), and gist tokens that compress prompt information through attention bottlenecks (Mu et al., 2023). BBC instead uses existing segment-end states as carriers.

Second, generation requires fine positional information: every token position remains potentially relevant to the next-token distribution. This appears to leave little room for structural compression. Yet positional detail need not imply arbitrary representational complexity. A sequence of hidden states may preserve every token position while still admitting a simple underlying trajectory. Motivated by this observation, we study Continuous Concept (CC), which encourages neighboring hidden states to vary smoothly (Figure 1(b)). We analyze a spectral structure–residual decomposition: low-frequency modes form the structured component, while CC energy bounds the high-frequency residual and its finite-precision index length under a shared coding convention.

On GPT-2 Small, BBC improves evaluation NLL by approximately 0.99%0.99\% at 300M training tokens, while BBC+CC improves it by 1.30%1.30\%. On a deeper GPT-2 Medium model, the gains are 1.11%1.11\% and 1.44%1.44\%, respectively. BBC is not explained by sparsity alone: same-density sliding-window and random sparse-attention controls do not reproduce its gain, and randomizing the location of BBC carriers significantly degrades performance. Similarly, CC is not explained by either of its two components. Their improvements also persist with longer training, reaching 1.12%1.12\% for BBC and 1.26%1.26\% for BBC+CC through our 20B-token runs.

Our empirical study also reveals that the two biases favor different depths. BBC works best near the bottom of the network, while CC is most effective at later layers. Interestingly, the depth asymmetry is consistent with the broader intuition that different depths of a Transformer perform different computational roles: earlier representations can benefit from compact cross-span structure, whereas later representations retain fine token-level access while benefiting from simpler feature geometry.

Our results suggest that scaling NTP is not the only lever for improving language-model training. Explicit biases on how information is represented can improve the same predictive objective.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We use the two-part coding principle to analyze structure–residual inductive biases in language-model representations.

  • •

    We introduce BBC, which compresses cross-segment communication through boundary carriers, and characterize CC as a spectral structure–residual bias with explicit reconstruction and residual-description bounds; their parameters KK and β\beta set the balance.

  • •

    We find that BBC and CC favor different depths, outperform matched architectural and regularization controls, and deliver gains that persist across model sizes and long training horizons; the KK and β\beta sweeps are U-shaped, consistent with this role.

2 The Structure–Residual Coding Principle

Two-part coding describes an object through its structure and the detail needed to identify its particular realization (Vereshchagin and Vitanyi, 2004). We write 𝖪\mathsf{K} for prefix Kolmogorov complexity. For finitely described objects,

𝖪⁡(X∣C)≤𝖪⁡(Z∣C)+𝖪⁡(X∣Z,C)+O⁡(1).\mathsf{K}(X\mid C)\leq\mathsf{K}(Z\mid C)+\mathsf{K}(X\mid Z,C)+O(1).

Here ZZ describes structure and the conditional term describes the remaining realization detail.

We use this principle to motivate concrete coding bounds. Let Γ\Gamma denote a coding convention shared by the encoder and decoder. Suppose that, after decoding ZZ, a residual codebook with Mδ​(Z)M_{\delta}(Z) entries permits reconstruction of XX to accuracy δ\delta. A two-part code then satisfies

ℓδSR​(X∣C,Γ)≤ℓstr​(Z∣C,Γ)+⌈log2⁡Mδ​(Z)⌉.\ell_{\delta}^{\mathrm{SR}}(X\mid C,\Gamma)\leq\ell_{\mathrm{str}}(Z\mid C,\Gamma)+\left\lceil\log_{2}M_{\delta}(Z)\right\rceil.

The structure code is self-delimiting, and the decoded structure and coding convention determine the residual index length. Any codebook or parameter not shared in advance must also be described.

For discrete objects, the residual codebook can enumerate realizations sharing a structure. For continuous representations, a covering codebook gives reconstruction at a chosen precision.

The bounds below concern these explicit codes; neither BBC nor CC directly optimizes Kolmogorov complexity.

BBC and CC implement different parts of this viewpoint. BBC restricts direct cross-segment communication while retaining local autoregressive detail; Section 3 shows that its segment length KK sets this restriction and that both extreme values of KK give the vanilla model. CC controls the residual outside a low-frequency representation of the hidden-state trajectory; Section 4 bounds this residual by the CC energy and relates the weight β\beta to the energy budget. Section 5 connects the two mechanisms, and Section 6 locates the best KK and β\beta empirically.

3 Boundary Bottleneck Concept

Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) instantiates the structure–residual principle through a granularity hyperparameter KK. A sequence is divided into segments of KK tokens. At a selected Transformer layer, each completed segment communicates with later segments only through its boundary state, while ordinary autoregressive computation is preserved inside the current segment.

Boundary-limited attention. For notational simplicity, assume that KK divides NN and index segments by i=0,…,N/K−1i=0,\ldots,N/K-1. Empty ranges in the attention mask are interpreted as empty sets.

For fixed segment length KK, define Si=(xi​K+1,…,x(i+1)​K)S_{i}=\left(x_{iK+1},\ldots,x_{(i+1)K}\right). The final position of each segment serves as its boundary carrier.

For a query token xtx_{t} in segment s=⌊t−1K⌋s=\left\lfloor\frac{t-1}{K}\right\rfloor, BBC replaces the ordinary causal attention pattern at the selected layer by

𝒜BBC​(t)={K,2​K,…,s​K}∪{s​K+1,…,t}.\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{BBC}}(t)=\{K,2K,\ldots,sK\}\cup\{sK+1,\ldots,t\}. (1)

Once a segment is completed, its KK token states are no longer independently accessible to later segments at the BBC layer. The current segment remains autoregressive. Let CsC_{s} denote the causal context preceding segment SsS_{s}, and define xs,r=xs​K+r+1x_{s,r}=x_{sK+r+1}. The segment distribution factorizes as pθ​(Ss∣Cs)=∏r=0K−1pθ​(xs,r∣Cs,xs,<r)p_{\theta}(S_{s}\mid C_{s})=\prod_{r=0}^{K-1}p_{\theta}\left(x_{s,r}\mid C_{s},x_{s,<r}\right).

All other layers retain the standard causal mask. Since other layers and the residual stream can retain additional prefix information, this layer-local restriction does not imply that the full model conditions only on boundary carriers.

Its realization class is 𝒮K​(a)={S′∈𝒱K:ϕ⁡(S′)=a}\mathcal{S}_{K}(a)=\{S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}^{K}:\phi(S^{\prime})=a\}, where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the vocabulary. The segment distribution induces a structure distribution: pθ​(a∣Cs)=∑S′∈𝒮K​(a)pθ​(S′∣Cs)p_{\theta}(a\mid C_{s})=\sum_{S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{K}(a)}p_{\theta}(S^{\prime}\mid C_{s}).

−log⁡pθ​(S∣Cs)=−log⁡pθ​(a∣Cs)−log⁡pθ​(S∣a,Cs).-\log p_{\theta}(S\mid C_{s})=-\log p_{\theta}(a\mid C_{s})-\log p_{\theta}(S\mid a,C_{s}). (2)

The realization class also gives a coding bound. 𝖪⁡(S∣Cs,ΓBBC)≤𝖪⁡(a∣Cs,ΓBBC)+⌈log2⁡|𝒮K​(a)|⌉+O⁡(1).\mathsf{K}(S\mid C_{s},\Gamma_{\mathrm{BBC}})\leq\mathsf{K}(a\mid C_{s},\Gamma_{\mathrm{BBC}})+\left\lceil\log_{2}|\mathcal{S}_{K}(a)|\right\rceil+O(1).

Proposition 1 (Segment length sets the bottleneck).

Fix NN and the BBC layer. For a query at position t≤Nt\leq N, write t=s​K+r+1t=sK+r+1 with s=⌊(t−1)/K⌋s=\lfloor(t-1)/K\rfloor and 0≤r≤K−10\leq r\leq K-1.

  1. (i)

    Routing. The query attends to the ss boundary carriers of the completed segments and to the r+1r+1 positions s​K+1,…,tsK+1,\ldots,t of its current segment. Relative to the causal mask, it loses direct access to exactly s⁡(K−1)s(K-1) positions, the non-boundary tokens of the completed segments.

  2. (ii)

    Endpoints. 𝒜BBC​(t)={1,…,t}\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{BBC}}(t)=\{1,\ldots,t\} for every t≤Nt\leq N if and only if K=1K=1 or K≥NK\geq N. In both cases the BBC layer is a standard causal attention layer.

  3. (iii)

    Structure and realization. The segment distribution admits the decomposition in Equation 2. Under the stated coding convention, a nonempty realization class requires at most ⌈log2⁡|𝒮K​(a)|⌉≤⌈K​log2​|𝒱|⌉\lceil\log_{2}|\mathcal{S}_{K}(a)|\rceil\leq\lceil K\log_{2}|\mathcal{V}|\rceil index bits.

Parts (i) and (ii) hold for every K≥1K\geq 1; the proof is in Appendix C.5.

By (i), KK sets the split at the BBC layer: each completed segment is visible there only through its boundary state, while up to KK positions of the current segment remain directly visible. A key δ≥1\delta\geq 1 tokens back is removed for a fraction (min⁡(δ,K)−1)/K(\min(\delta,K)-1)/K of query offsets, so from distance KK on exactly one key in KK remains: KK sets a distance scale, not only a sparsity level (Lemma 2, Appendix C.6). By (ii), K=1K=1 and K≥NK\geq N give the vanilla model.

The probability identities hold for any segment distribution; BBC contributes the architectural routing restriction. Its structure–residual interpretation is therefore a compact cross-segment carrier together with retained local autoregressive computation. The boundary need not equal ϕ⁡(S)\phi(S) or be predictively sufficient by construction.

4 Continuous Concept

Continuous Concept (CC) is an optimization bias on the geometry of the hidden-state trajectory. Let N≥2N\geq 2, and let H∈ℝN×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} have row ii equal to hi⊤h_{i}^{\top}. The states are taken at a selected layer. CC penalizes adjacent variation:

ℒCC=1N−1​∑i=1N−1‖hi+1−hi‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\|h_{i+1}-h_{i}\|_{2}^{2}.

The objective is ℒ=ℒNTP+β​ℒCC\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NTP}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}}, where β≥0\beta\geq 0 controls the regularization strength. In our implementation, ℒCC\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}} is also averaged over the dd hidden coordinates, so each reported β\beta equals dd times the coefficient defined here; the same holds for ℒscale\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{scale}} and ℒCC​-​2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC\text{-}2}} in Section 6.

We analyze the trajectory as low-frequency structure plus a high-frequency residual. The CC objective controls an upper bound on the residual magnitude.

Spectral structure and residual. Let LL be the unit-weight path Laplacian. The unnormalized CC energy is E⁡(H)=∑i=1N−1‖hi+1−hi‖22=Tr⁡(H⊤​L​H)=(N−1)​ℒCCE(H)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\|h_{i+1}-h_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(H^{\top}LH)=(N-1)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}}. Write L=Q​Λ​Q⊤, 0=λ1<λ2≤⋯≤λNL=Q\Lambda Q^{\top},\ 0=\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{N}, with orthonormal eigenvectors. These form a graph-frequency basis over token positions (Shuman et al., 2013). This is a vector-valued path instance of the graph-smoothness objective underlying Laplacian Eigenmaps (Belkin and Niyogi, 2003).

For 1≤m<N1\leq m<N, define Qm=[q1,…,qm],Hm=Qm​Qm⊤​HQ_{m}=[q_{1},\ldots,q_{m}],\ H_{m}=Q_{m}Q_{m}^{\top}H. HmH_{m} is the low-frequency structure, and Rm=H−HmR_{m}=H-H_{m} is the spectral residual.

Proposition 2 (Spectral residual bound).

For 1≤m<N,‖Rm‖F2≤E⁡(H)λm+11\leq m<N,\ \|R_{m}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{E(H)}{\lambda_{m+1}}.

Proof.

Let H^=Q⊤​H\widehat{H}=Q^{\top}H. Orthogonality gives ‖Rm‖F2=∑r>m‖H^r‖22,E⁡(H)=∑rλr​‖H^r‖22\|R_{m}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{r>m}\|\widehat{H}_{r}\|_{2}^{2},\ E(H)=\sum_{r}\lambda_{r}\|\widehat{H}_{r}\|_{2}^{2}. Therefore ‖Rm‖F2≤1λm+1​∑r>mλr​‖H^r‖22≤E⁡(H)λm+1\|R_{m}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{m+1}}\sum_{r>m}\lambda_{r}\|\widehat{H}_{r}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{E(H)}{\lambda_{m+1}}. ∎

For a chosen cutoff, the approximation is accurate when E⁡(H)/λm+1E(H)/\lambda_{m+1} is small.

Residual codebook size. Fix the dimensions, cutoff, and an energy budget E⋆≥0E_{\star}\geq 0. For trajectories with E⁡(H)≤E⋆E(H)\leq E_{\star}, the residual lies in a subspace of dimension D=(N−m)​dD=(N-m)d and in a ball of radius r⋆=E⋆λm+1r_{\star}=\sqrt{\frac{E_{\star}}{\lambda_{m+1}}}. A DD-dimensional Euclidean ball of radius r⋆r_{\star} admits a cover by at most

(1+2​r⋆η)D\left(1+\frac{2r_{\star}}{\eta}\right)^{D} (4)

balls of radius η>0\eta>0 (Vershynin, 2018).

Proposition 3 (Spectral residual index length).

For a shared covering codebook satisfying Equation 4, the bit length of an index identifying a residual approximation with Frobenius error at most η\eta satisfies

Lη​(Rm∣Γ)≤⌈(N−m)​d​log2⁡(1+2η​E⋆λm+1)⌉.L_{\eta}(R_{m}\mid\Gamma)\leq\left\lceil(N-m)d\log_{2}\left(1+\frac{2}{\eta}\sqrt{\frac{E_{\star}}{\lambda_{m+1}}}\right)\right\rceil.
Proof.

Choose a covering center within distance η\eta of the residual and transmit its index; Equation 4 then gives the bound. ∎

The coding convention Γ\Gamma includes the dimensions, basis, cutoff, energy budget, precision, and codebook; any unshared components incur additional description cost. Allocating reconstruction error δ/2\delta/2 to both structure and residual gives ‖H−(H~m+R~m)‖F≤δ\|H-(\widetilde{H}_{m}+\widetilde{R}_{m})\|_{F}\leq\delta, and hence

ℓδSR​(H∣Γ)≤ℓδ/2str​(Hm∣Γ)+⌈(N−m)​d​log2⁡(1+4​r⋆δ)⌉.\ell_{\delta}^{\mathrm{SR}}(H\mid\Gamma)\leq\ell_{\delta/2}^{\mathrm{str}}(H_{m}\mid\Gamma)+\left\lceil(N-m)d\log_{2}\left(1+\frac{4r_{\star}}{\delta}\right)\right\rceil.

Thus, at fixed dimensions, cutoff, and precision, a smaller energy budget reduces the residual description bound, while the structure retains its own description cost. A larger β\beta never increases the CC energy of the optimal model (Appendix C.7). Its strength at layer ll is κl=β​ρl\kappa_{l}=\beta\rho_{l}, where ρl\rho_{l} is the ratio of the CC to the NTP gradient (Appendix C.8).

5 From spectral smoothness to boundary representation

The structure–residual coding viewpoint motivates both interventions. We now give a qualitative connection: low within-segment path energy bounds the error of multiplicity-corrected boundary attention (Appendix B.3 tests it on trained layers). The reverse direction requires additional conditions; see Appendix B.

Proposition 4 (Multiplicity-corrected boundary attention).

Let Δs=maxj⁡|gj−g~j|,Δv=maxj⁡‖uj−u~j‖2\Delta_{s}=\max_{j}|g_{j}-\widetilde{g}_{j}|,\ \Delta_{v}=\max_{j}\|u_{j}-\widetilde{u}_{j}\|_{2}. If ‖u~j‖2≤Vmax\|\widetilde{u}_{j}\|_{2}\leq V_{\max} for every group, including local-prefix singletons, then

For fixed KK and uniformly bounded sensitivity and value constants, the error vanishes as the maximum segment energy vanishes. This is a same-layer result for multiplicity-corrected attention, not directly for the uncorrected BBC mask. The bound assumes that hih_{i} enters the stated key and value maps; intervening normalization must be included in the sensitivity constants, and position-dependent maps or logit biases require additional terms. Appendix C.9 gives these terms for rotary position embeddings, for this result and for Proposition 6; our GPT-2 models use learned absolute position embeddings and need no such term.

6 Experiments

Setup. We pre-train gpt2-small and gpt2-medium models (Radford et al., 2019) with context length N=1024N=1024 on a randomly sampled 1B-token subset of FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024). We evaluate on a 1M-token holdout set sampled from the same dataset and report holdout NLL. The primary runs use a cosine learning-rate schedule over 1B tokens with a 5M-token linear warmup. To reduce compute, hyperparameter sweeps and ablations are evaluated after 100M or 300M training tokens while retaining the same 1B-token learning-rate decay schedule. Unless otherwise noted, we use three seeds, {82,23,37}\{82,23,37\}, and report mean and standard deviation. For the 20B-token runs, we enlarge the holdout set to 10M tokens and use a single seed (82) to reduce computational cost.

We first tune the vanilla baseline by sweeping the learning rate η∈{3×10−4,6×10−4,10−3,1.5×10−3}\eta\in\{3\times 10^{-4},6\times 10^{-4},10^{-3},1.5\times 10^{-3}\}. We then fix η\eta and separately sweep the BBC segment length K∈{4,8,16,32,64}K\in\{4,8,16,32,64\} and the CC regularization strength β∈{0.005,0.0025,0.00125,0.000625}\beta\in\{0.005,0.0025,0.00125,0.000625\}. We do not retune η\eta for BBC or CC, avoiding method-specific learning-rate tuning. We use η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} for gpt2-small and η=6×10−4\eta=6\times 10^{-4} for gpt2-medium.

BBC and CC are depth-dependent. Our first finding is a clear depth dependence for both methods. We sweep the intervention layer over the even-numbered Transformer layers for both gpt2-small and gpt2-medium, using K∈{4,8,16}K\in\{4,8,16\} for BBC and β∈{0.00125,0.0025,0.005}\beta\in\{0.00125,0.0025,0.005\} for CC (Figure 2 and also Table 2, 3 in Appendix A.1). The same qualitative pattern appears across both model sizes: BBC is most effective when applied at lower layers, whereas CC becomes more effective toward higher layers. This depth asymmetry was not built into either method. Interestingly, it is consistent with the motivating intuition that BBC is perception-inspired while CC is generation-inspired, suggesting that different Transformer depths may favor different representational functions.

In the main BBC/CC comparisons, BBC is applied at layer 2, while CC is applied at layer 10 for gpt2-small and layer 22 for gpt2-medium.

Optimal KK and β\beta. We sweep KK and β\beta over broad ranges to identify their optimal values. As shown in Figure 3, both exhibit approximately U-shaped performance curves with relatively broad optima: K∈[8,32]K\in[8,32] and β∈[0.00125,0.0025]\beta\in[0.00125,0.0025] (Tables 2–5). For β\beta, the best strength β⋆​ρl\beta^{\star}\rho_{l} (Section 4), fitted on medium layers 10–20, predicts β⋆=0.0013\beta^{\star}=0.0013 at layer 22 for GPT2 Medium and 0.00210.0021 at layer 10 for GPT2 Small; the sweeps find 0.001250.00125 and 0.00250.0025 (Table 21).

300M significance tests and 1B persistence. We find that the best KK and β\beta selected at 100M tokens retain their gains through 1B training tokens. For gpt2-small, we use K=8K=8 and β=0.0025\beta=0.0025. For gpt2-medium, we use K=16K=16 and β=0.00125\beta=0.00125.

At 300M tokens, the ordering is consistent across both model sizes: CC significantly outperforms vanilla, BBC significantly outperforms CC, and BBC+CC significantly outperforms BBC (Figure 4(a) and also Table 6, 7 in Appendix A.3 for pp-values).

The improvement persists as training continues. As shown in Figure 4(b), from 300M to 1B tokens, BBC shows a steady upward trend in relative improvement over vanilla for both gpt2-small and gpt2-medium, while BBC+CC continues to maintain a statistically significant margin over BBC.

BBC is not merely sparse attention. BBC is a sparse attention pattern. To test whether its gains arise simply from reduced attention density, we compare BBC against same-density sliding-window and random sparse attention, applying all sparse patterns at layer 2. At 100M tokens, BBC significantly outperforms both baselines, and neither of them improves over the vanilla baseline (Figure 5(a)).

We further compare against Random BBC, in which the carrier positions are selected at random while preserving the same per-token attention budget. At 300M tokens, BBC significantly outperforms Random BBC (Figure 5(b)), indicating that the gain depends on structured carrier placement rather than the attention budget alone. Table 8 in Appendix A.4 reports the paired tt-test pp-values.

CC requires both scale and roughness. The CC objective has a natural tendency to reduce hidden-state scale (see Appendix C.1 for a formal discussion). To test whether its gains arise primarily from this scaling effect, we compare against a scale regularizer, ℒscale=1N​∑i=1N∥hi∥22\mathcal{L}_{\rm scale}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lVert h_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}, and a normalized roughness regularizer, ℒnorm=1N−1​∑i=1N−1∥hi+1−hi∥22∥hi+1∥22+∥hi∥22+ε\mathcal{L}_{\rm norm}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\frac{\lVert h_{i+1}-h_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\lVert h_{i+1}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert h_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\varepsilon}. The normalized roughness term is complementary to scale in the CC objective.

CC is based on the path-graph Laplacian, whose Dirichlet energy is the weakest penalty in the finite-range pairwise family considered here (see Appendix C.2). We also include CC-2 ℒCC​-​2=1N−2​∑i=1N−2∥2​hi+2−hi+1−hi∥22\mathcal{L}_{\rm CC\text{-}2}=\frac{1}{N-2}\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}\lVert 2h_{i+2}-h_{i+1}-h_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}, a two-predecessor Laplacian-residual penalty, in the ablation study. CC is also closely related to cosine distance (see Appendix C.4), which is included as well.

We tune the application layer and β\beta separately for each variant (Table 9, 10, 11, and 12 in Appendix A.5). As shown in Figure 5, CC significantly outperforms all of these variants. Table 13 in Appendix A.5 reports the corresponding paired tt-test pp-values.

20B training runs. We next extend training to 20B tokens. We find that changing the learning-rate decay horizon also changes the optimal CC weight β\beta. Following the same low-cost tuning strategy used in the 1B-token experiments, we select β\beta using a 1B-token run and find that its gain persists through 20B tokens (Figure 1(c)).

During the 20B runs, however, BBC+CC temporarily underperforms BBC at intermediate checkpoints. We hypothesize that this is partly a numerical-stability issue: because β≪1\beta\ll 1, the effective contribution of the CC term can become numerically negligible as ℒCC\mathcal{L}_{\rm CC} decreases during training.

We therefore study two variants: random dropout, which randomly omits the CC term on a fraction of optimization steps, and adaptive dropout, which omits the CC term when its value falls below the pp-th percentile of the preceding hh-step history. The latter is designed to avoid repeatedly applying very small CC updates that may vanish after scaling by β\beta. With adaptive dropout, BBC+CC consistently outperforms BBC at every intermediate checkpoint (see Table 15 and Figure 7 in Appendix A.6).

Representation diagnostics. The preceding experiments establish that BBC and CC improve next-token prediction. We next ask whether the learned representations change in the directions suggested by Sections 3 and 4.

To test whether BBC increases the relative importance of boundary representations, we either replace the boundary representation and measure the resulting NLL increase, Δb\Delta_{b}, or replace a randomly selected non-boundary representation and measure the corresponding increase, Δi\Delta_{i}. A larger Δb−Δi\Delta_{b}-\Delta_{i} indicates that boundary representations are relatively more consequential for prediction. With both zero-vector replacement and replacement by the mean of the preceding K−1K-1 hidden states, BBC yields a significantly larger Δb−Δi\Delta_{b}-\Delta_{i} than Vanilla (Table 1). In both experiments, we exclude the first W=4W=4 segments to control for the disproportionate influence of initial-token positions (see Appendix A.7 for full diagnostic).

Next we test whether reducing CC energy makes the hidden-state trajectory better approximated by its low-frequency path-graph modes. For each hidden-state trajectory HH, we project onto the first mm path-graph eigenmodes, Hm=Qm​Qm⊤​HH_{m}=Q_{m}Q_{m}^{\top}H, and measure the normalized spectral residual ρm​(H)=‖H−Hm‖F2‖H‖F2\rho_{m}(H)=\frac{\|H-H_{m}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|H\|_{F}^{2}}. This ratio is invariant to uniform rescaling and measures the residual relative to total hidden-state energy. It includes the constant positional component; it does not isolate roughness of the centered trajectory. CC reduces ρm​(H)\rho_{m}(H) at every measured spectral cutoff. Across the measured range, this corresponds to a relative reduction of approximately 22%22\%–28%28\% (Figure 6 and Table 16 in Appendix A.8).

RoPE. GPT-2 uses absolute positional embeddings, whereas most modern LLMs use rotary positional embeddings (RoPE; Su et al., 2024). To test whether BBC and CC are robust to the choice of positional encoding, we additionally train Pythia-410M (Biderman et al., 2023), a GPT-2-like model using RoPE. We reuse the gpt2-medium hyperparameters without retuning (η=6×10−4\eta=6\times 10^{-4}, K=16K=16, and β=0.00125\beta=0.00125), and train for 1B tokens. BBC improves evaluation NLL by 0.58%, while BBC+CC improves it by 0.83%, suggesting that the gains are not specific to absolute positional embeddings (Table 17 in Appendix A.9). We also sweep rotary_pct, which controls the fraction of head dimensions using rotary embeddings, over {0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}. The default value, 0.250.25, also performs best for Pythia-410M (Table 18 in Appendix A.9). RoPE modifies the attention mechanism; Appendix C.9 extends Proposition 4 to rotary positional encoding.

7 Related Work

Representation learning for LLMs. Representation learning has been central to self-supervised learning in vision, where joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) (Assran et al., 2023) learn semantic representations through embedding-space prediction. Recent work brings related ideas to language: LLM-JEPA (Huang et al., 2026a) incorporates JEPA-style objectives into language-model training, while Semantic Tube Prediction (STP) (Huang et al., 2026b) introduces a geometric prior on hidden-state trajectories. Large Concept Models (LCM Team et al., 2024) perform autoregressive prediction in a sentence-level embedding space. Our work shares the general motivation and introduces principled structure–residual inductive biases.

Structured communication. Fixed sparse attention (Child et al., 2019) combines local attention with access to positions near previous block boundaries. BBC can be viewed as a single-carrier (c=1c=1) specialization—a setting that Child et al. (2019) found overly restrictive—but we show that applying it at the appropriate depth improves predictive performance. Block Transformer (Ho et al., 2024) places global block processing below local token decoding. Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2025) compresses context into inserted beacon tokens’ key–value states. H-Net (Hwang et al., 2026) learns boundaries, processes selected states at reduced resolution, and upsamples for decoding. Local, random, and global connections are standard ingredients of sparse attention designs such as Big Bird (Zaheer et al., 2020) and Landmark Attention (Mohtashami and Jaggi, 2023).

Smoothness and spectral structure. AWD-LSTM (Merity et al., 2018) penalizes successive recurrent-state changes through temporal activation regularization. Li et al. (2026) encourage angular dispersion across batchwise hidden states. Shuman et al. (2013) express graph smoothness through Laplacian frequencies. CC regularizes adjacent Transformer hidden states and bounds low-frequency reconstruction error and finite-precision residual code length, with ablations separating scale from positional roughness.

Two-part coding. CRATE (Yu et al., 2023b) alternates token compression and feature sparsification; ToST (Wu et al., 2025) derives attention by unrolling variational coding-rate reduction. Delétang et al. (2024) turn predictive probabilities into lossless data codes. Minimum description length (Rissanen, 1978) charges for the model and data encoded under it, while algorithmic statistics (Gács et al., 2001) formalizes structure and realization through two-part codes. We adopt this two-part accounting for BBC’s segment realizations and CC’s spectral representations, retaining both structure and residual costs without directly optimizing Kolmogorov complexity.

Depth specialization. Skean et al. (2025) evaluate layerwise geometry and information content for embedding quality. Lad et al. (2025) probe computational sensitivity by deleting and swapping layers. Our training-time layer sweeps identify early BBC and late CC as favorable placements in two GPT-2 model sizes; these preferences are observed empirically, not prescribed by the methods.

8 Conclusion

Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we introduced BBC and CC as complementary structure–residual inductive biases for language-model pretraining and derived explicit bounds characterizing both mechanisms. BBC compresses cross-segment communication through boundary carriers, while CC encourages compact spectral structure in hidden-state trajectories. We further give a qualitative connection between the two and find that BBC favors early layers, whereas CC favors later layers. Their gains persist across model sizes and training horizons up to 20B tokens, demonstrating that explicit representation biases can improve next-token pretraining.

Appendix A Additional Experimental Results

A.1 BBC and CC are depth-dependent

Unlike BBC, which is applied within a Transformer layer, CC regularizes the hidden state between layers. To avoid introducing a layer index of −1-1, we index CC by the layer whose input it regularizes. Under this convention, the output of the final layer can be viewed as the input to a phantom layer N+1N+1. We therefore sweep layers 0,2,…,12{0,2,\dots,12} for gpt2-small and 0,2,…,24{0,2,\dots,24} for gpt2-medium in Table 3.

A.6 20B Training Runs

When extending training to 20B tokens, we first retune the CC weight β\beta using a 1B-token sweep. Under the longer schedule, the slower learning-rate decay allows CC to exert greater cumulative downward pressure on ℒCC\mathcal{L}_{\rm CC}, which can shift the optimal β\beta. Using a single seed (82), we find that β=0.000625\beta=0.000625 performs best at 1B tokens. With this setting, BBC+CC eventually outperforms BBC after 10B tokens, but underperforms it at intermediate checkpoints between 4B and 9B tokens. Further decreasing β\beta does not improve the 1B-token result.

We hypothesize that this behavior is partly due to numerical stability: as ℒCC\mathcal{L}_{\rm CC} decreases, multiplying it by β≪1\beta\ll 1 can make the corresponding optimization signal numerically negligible. We therefore study two variants. Random dropout skips the CC term independently with dropout rate d>0d>0. Adaptive dropout instead skips the CC term whenever ℒCC\mathcal{L}_{\rm CC} falls below the pp-th percentile of its values over the preceding hh optimization steps, reducing the frequency of very small CC updates.

At 1B training tokens, we evaluate random dropout with d=0.5d=0.5 and adaptive dropout with p=50p=50 and h=32h=32 using three seeds {82,23,37}\{82,23,37\} (Table 14). Both variants substantially reduce the across-seed variance relative to standard CC, and adaptive dropout achieves the best mean performance of the three. We therefore use adaptive dropout for a second 20B-token run, where BBC+CC Adapt outperforms BBC at every intermediate checkpoint.

We evaluate every 1B-token intermediate checkpoint on an enlarged 10M-token holdout set to reduce evaluation noise. This gives the high precision required for comparing CC variants (Table 14) and offsets the absence of seed averaging in the single-seed 20B-token runs (Table 15). In addition, we evaluate on the 1M-token holdout set every 10M training tokens, which produces Figure 7.

A.7 Boundary Intervention Diagnostic

To test whether BBC increases the relative importance of boundary representations, we evaluate frozen 100M-token Vanilla and BBC checkpoints using two matched activation interventions. For each completed segment, we either replace the boundary representation by a zero vector and measure the resulting increase in NLL, denoted Δb\Delta_{b}, or replace a randomly selected non-boundary representation in the same segment and measure the corresponding increase, denoted Δi\Delta_{i}. We use

G=Δb−ΔiG=\Delta_{b}-\Delta_{i} (5)

as the boundary-preference statistic. A positive GG indicates that ablating the boundary is more damaging than ablating a matched interior position. More importantly,

GBBC>GVanillaG_{\mathrm{BBC}}>G_{\mathrm{Vanilla}} (6)

indicates that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary representations.

Controlling for early-position effects.

A direct intervention over the entire sequence is confounded by the unusually large influence of the first few tokens. Figure 8 shows the boundary-preference statistic as the ablated interior position is moved relative to the segment boundary. With K=8K=8, position −7-7 corresponds to the first token of a segment. Without excluding the initial segments, ablating this position produces a disproportionately large change in NLL, dominating the boundary-versus-interior comparison.

We therefore exclude the first W=4W=4 segments from both the intervention statistics and the corresponding NLL evaluation. After this warmup exclusion, the dependence on the particular non-boundary position becomes negligible (Figure 8), allowing the diagnostic to isolate the relative effect of boundary placement rather than the special role of the earliest tokens.

Zero-vector intervention.

With W=4W=4, we obtain

Model Δb\Delta_{b} Δi\Delta_{i} Δb−Δi\Delta_{b}-\Delta_{i}
Vanilla 1.2293±0.15661.2293\pm 0.1566 1.2318±0.15561.2318\pm 0.1556 −0.0025±0.0618-0.0025\pm 0.0618
BBC 0.8553±0.10280.8553\pm 0.1028 0.8500±0.10260.8500\pm 0.1026 0.0052±0.05890.0052\pm 0.0589

Vanilla exhibits essentially no positive boundary preference: Δb−Δi=−0.0025\Delta_{b}-\Delta_{i}=-0.0025. In contrast, BBC yields a positive boundary-preference gap of 0.00520.0052. More importantly, the paired BBC–Vanilla contrast is statistically significant,

t⁡(1023)=4.160,p=3.46×10−5.t(1023)=4.160,\qquad p=3.46\times 10^{-5}. (7)

Thus BBC significantly increases the relative sensitivity of the model to boundary representations compared with matched interior representations.

Mean-replacement intervention.

To verify that the result is not specific to zero-vector ablation, we repeat the experiment using a less disruptive intervention: the selected representation is replaced by the mean of the preceding K−1K-1 hidden states. We obtain

Model Δb\Delta_{b} Δi\Delta_{i} Δb−Δi\Delta_{b}-\Delta_{i}
Vanilla 0.6267±0.06830.6267\pm 0.0683 0.6251±0.06700.6251\pm 0.0670 0.0017±0.06260.0017\pm 0.0626
BBC 0.5612±0.06360.5612\pm 0.0636 0.5546±0.06160.5546\pm 0.0616 0.0065±0.05840.0065\pm 0.0584

The Vanilla gap is small relative to its per-example variability, whereas BBC again exhibits a larger positive boundary preference. The paired contrast is significant:

t⁡(1023)=3.499,p=4.86×10−4.t(1023)=3.499,\qquad p=4.86\times 10^{-4}. (8)

Taken together, the two interventions give the same qualitative result: standard next-token training shows little or no systematic preference for the fixed segment boundaries used by BBC, whereas BBC significantly increases the relative predictive importance of those boundary representations. This provides direct representation-level evidence that the BBC routing constraint causes useful information to become preferentially concentrated at the designated carrier positions.

Appendix B Additional Connections Between BBC and CC

We now consider the reverse direction. BBC restricts the value subspace available for cross-segment communication. Smoothness requires an additional condition on how attention changes between neighboring queries.

B.1 Cross-segment feature subspace

Consider one deterministic attention head. Let BB be the union of boundary positions available to the queries, assigning zero weights to inaccessible positions. Let

AB∈ℝNq×|B|,VB∈ℝ|B|×dv.A_{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times|B|},\qquad V_{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{|B|\times d_{v}}.

The cross-segment contribution is

Ocross=AB​VB.O_{\mathrm{cross}}=A_{B}V_{B}. (9)

Rows of ABA_{B} need not sum to one, because local-prefix tokens also receive attention.

Proposition 5 (Cross-segment subspace constraint).
rank⁡(Ocross)≤min⁡(Nq,|B|,dv),\operatorname{rank}(O_{\mathrm{cross}})\leq\min(N_{q},|B|,d_{v}), (10)

and every output row belongs to span⁡{vb:b∈B}\operatorname{span}\{v_{b}:b\in B\}.

Proof.

Each row of AB​VBA_{B}V_{B} is a linear combination of boundary values, and the rank of a product cannot exceed the rank of either factor. ∎

This constrains one head’s cross-segment contribution, rather than the complete hidden state. The carrier-count bound need not tighten the value-dimension bound when |B|≥dv|B|\geq d_{v}. Nor does low rank imply smoothness: alternating rows u,−u,u,−u,…u,-u,u,-u,\ldots have rank one and adjacent energy 4​(Nq−1)​‖u‖224(N_{q}-1)\|u\|_{2}^{2}.

B.2 Conditional smoothness

For the adjacent-difference operator DD,

‖D​Ocross‖F2≤‖VB‖op2​‖D​AB‖F2.\|DO_{\mathrm{cross}}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|V_{B}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\|DA_{B}\|_{F}^{2}. (11)

Thus similar boundary-attention weights yield similar cross-segment outputs.

For this comparison, restrict BB to the fixed, nonempty set of boundaries preceding one segment. Let KB∈ℝ|B|×dkK_{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{|B|\times d_{k}} contain their keys as rows, and restrict VBV_{B} to the same positions. Assume boundary logits qi⊤​kb/dkq_{i}^{\top}k_{b}/\sqrt{d_{k}}. Define the boundary-normalized distribution and total boundary attention mass:

a¯i=softmax⁡(KB​qidk),γi=∑b∈B(AB)i​b.\overline{a}_{i}=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{K_{B}q_{i}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right),\qquad\gamma_{i}=\sum_{b\in B}(A_{B})_{ib}. (12)

Then

zi=VB⊤​a¯i,oicross=γi​zi.z_{i}=V_{B}^{\top}\overline{a}_{i},\qquad o_{i}^{\mathrm{cross}}=\gamma_{i}z_{i}. (13)

Here 0≤γi≤10\leq\gamma_{i}\leq 1; the remaining attention mass belongs to the local prefix.

Write EintraE_{\mathrm{intra}} for adjacent energy restricted to this segment, and let QqryQ^{\mathrm{qry}} be the query matrix. Set

Vmax=maxb∈B⁡‖vb‖2,CB=‖VB‖op​‖KB‖op2​dk.V_{\max}=\max_{b\in B}\|v_{b}\|_{2},\qquad C_{B}=\frac{\|V_{B}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|K_{B}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{2\sqrt{d_{k}}}.
Proposition 6 (Conditional BBC-to-CC smoothness).

For fixed boundary keys and values,

Eintra​(Ocross)≤(Vmax​Eintra​(γ)+CB​Eintra​(Qqry))2.\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{intra}}(O_{\mathrm{cross}})\leq\bigl(V_{\max}\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{intra}}(\gamma)}+C_{B}\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{intra}}(Q^{\mathrm{qry}})}\bigr)^{2}. (14)
Proof.

The softmax Jacobian is J=diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤J=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}. It is symmetric and has absolute row sums 2​pi​(1−pi)≤1/22p_{i}(1-p_{i})\leq 1/2, so its Euclidean operator norm is at most 1/21/2. Thus

‖zi+1−zi‖2≤CB​‖qi+1−qi‖2.\|z_{i+1}-z_{i}\|_{2}\leq C_{B}\|q_{i+1}-q_{i}\|_{2}.

The triangle inequality over consecutive differences gives the result. ∎

Both terms matter. With one boundary value uu, zero local values, and identical zero logits, the cross-segment output changes from u/2u/2 to u/3u/3 when the local prefix grows from one token to two, even with identical queries.

BBC therefore transfers smoothness when both queries and total boundary attention mass vary smoothly. Transitions between segments, where the boundary set changes, require a separate term.

B.3 Proposition 4 at trained BBC layers

We test Proposition 4 at the BBC layer (layer 2) of two models trained for 1B tokens: gpt2-medium with K=16K=16 and learned position embeddings, and Pythia-410M with K=16K=16 and rotary embeddings. We use the queries, keys and values of the first 100k held-out tokens (98 and 50 sequences, all 16 heads, 256 random queries per sequence). Since the key and value maps are already applied, we use Lemma 1 on the key and value paths themselves: |gj−g~j|≤‖q‖2​(K−1)​EjK/dk|g_{j}-\widetilde{g}_{j}|\leq\|q\|_{2}\sqrt{(K-1)E^{K}_{j}}/\sqrt{d_{k}} and ‖uj−u~j‖2≤(K−1)​EjV\|u_{j}-\widetilde{u}_{j}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{(K-1)E^{V}_{j}}, where EjKE^{K}_{j} and EjVE^{V}_{j} are the path energies of the keys and values in segment jj. For Pythia we use the keys before rotation and add the rotary term of Appendix C.9. Because ‖W⁡(hi−hb)‖2≤‖W‖op​‖hi−hb‖2\|W(h_{i}-h_{b})\|_{2}\leq\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|h_{i}-h_{b}\|_{2}, this version is never weaker than the one stated with cKc_{K}, cVc_{V} and the path energy of hh. Every inequality in the chain holds on all sampled queries.

Table 19 shows that the low-energy condition does not hold. Inside a segment the values are as rough as a random reordering of the same tokens, and the keys are only somewhat smoother in gpt2-medium. The logit radius implied by the path energy is about 150 nats, so tanh\tanh saturates and the bound exceeds 2​Vmax2V_{\max} for every query. With the measured Δs\Delta_{s} and Δv\Delta_{v} the bound is tighter but still vacuous for almost all queries, and it does not rank queries by their error. The cause is that the logit gaps themselves are large: the measured Δs\Delta_{s} has median 10.8 and 12.6 nats, so tanh⁡(Δs)≈1\tanh(\Delta_{s})\approx 1 and the bound is close to Δv+2​Vmax\Delta_{v}+2V_{\max} for almost every query, whatever the actual error. Across the 16 Pythia heads, the bound and the median error have rank correlation −0.72-0.72.

The error is governed instead by the attention mass that the mask removes. Let mm be the dense attention mass on keys outside the BBC pattern and u¯M\bar{u}_{M} the attention-weighted mean of their values. Dense attention restricted to the visible keys equals (1−m)​oBBC(1-m)\,o_{\mathrm{BBC}}, so o−oBBC=m⁡(u¯M−oBBC)o-o_{\mathrm{BBC}}=m(\bar{u}_{M}-o_{\mathrm{BBC}}) exactly, and mm ranks queries by their error far better than the bound. In gpt2-medium, dense attention with the same qq and kk would put almost all of its mass outside the BBC pattern, spread over hundreds of positions. With rotary embeddings the logits stay local and mm is small. A trained BBC layer can therefore rely on the mask for locality; it does not have to approximate a dense layer. We read Proposition 4 as a qualitative continuity result, not as a quantitative estimate for trained models. The Pythia results are the same with K=8K=8 and K=32K=32.

At layer 2 the mask deletes most of the vanilla layer’s attention for every KK from 4 to 64, and in both models the three values of KK with the best NLL delete the most. Across the swept layers, the rank correlation between ml​(8)m_{l}(8) and the BBC NLL of Table 2 is −0.43-0.43 for gpt2-small and −0.08-0.08 for gpt2-medium. A trained BBC layer therefore does not approximate the vanilla layer; it uses the mask to restructure access, in line with Appendix B.3.

Lemma 3 (CC energy is monotone in β\beta).

Fix the model class and the training distribution. For β≥0\beta\geq 0, let θβ\theta_{\beta} minimize ℒNTP+β​ℒCC\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NTP}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}}. Moreover, θβ\theta_{\beta} minimizes ℒNTP\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NTP}} among all models with ℒCC≤ℒCC​(θβ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}}\leq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}}(\theta_{\beta}).

Proof.

Write f=ℒNTPf=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NTP}}, g=ℒCCg=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CC}} and θk=θβk\theta_{k}=\theta_{\beta_{k}}. Optimality gives f⁡(θ1)+β1​g​(θ1)≤f⁡(θ2)+β1​g​(θ2)f(\theta_{1})+\beta_{1}g(\theta_{1})\leq f(\theta_{2})+\beta_{1}g(\theta_{2}) and f⁡(θ2)+β2​g​(θ2)≤f⁡(θ1)+β2​g​(θ1)f(\theta_{2})+\beta_{2}g(\theta_{2})\leq f(\theta_{1})+\beta_{2}g(\theta_{1}). Adding them yields (β2−β1)​(g⁡(θ2)−g⁡(θ1))≤0(\beta_{2}-\beta_{1})\bigl(g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})\bigr)\leq 0, so g⁡(θ2)≤g⁡(θ1)g(\theta_{2})\leq g(\theta_{1}). If a model θ\theta had g⁡(θ)≤g⁡(θβ)g(\theta)\leq g(\theta_{\beta}) and f⁡(θ)<f⁡(θβ)f(\theta)<f(\theta_{\beta}), its penalized objective would be smaller than that of θβ\theta_{\beta}. ∎

The lemma concerns exact minimizers, which training does not reach. Lower energy can also come from smaller scale, since E⁡(α​H)=α2​E​(H)E(\alpha H)=\alpha^{2}E(H) while R⁡(α​H)=R⁡(H)R(\alpha H)=R(H) (Appendix C.1), so the lemma alone does not show that β\beta shifts the balance between structure and residual. The following model makes this dependence explicit; it is graph Tikhonov smoothing (Shuman et al., 2013, Example 2) applied to hidden-state trajectories.

Proposition 9 (CC as a low-pass filter).

Treat HH as a free variable, as in Appendix C.1. Fix H0∈ℝN×dH_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} that is not constant across positions, and let μ>0\mu>0. For β≥0\beta\geq 0, the unique minimizer of μ2​‖H−H0‖F2+βN−1​E​(H)\frac{\mu}{2}\|H-H_{0}\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\beta}{N-1}E(H) is

H⋆​(β)=(I+τ​L)−1​H0,τ=2​βμ⁡(N−1),H^{\star}(\beta)=(I+\tau L)^{-1}H_{0},\qquad\tau=\frac{2\beta}{\mu(N-1)},

so the rr-th graph-frequency component of H0H_{0} is scaled by 1/(1+τ​λr)1/(1+\tau\lambda_{r}). For 1≤m<N1\leq m<N, the centered residual share ρmc​(β)=‖Rm​(H⋆​(β))‖F2/‖H⋆​(β)c‖F2\rho^{c}_{m}(\beta)=\|R_{m}(H^{\star}(\beta))\|_{F}^{2}/\|H^{\star}(\beta)_{c}\|_{F}^{2} is non-increasing in β\beta. The objective is strictly convex with gradient μ⁡(H−H0)+2​βN−1​L​H\mu(H-H_{0})+\frac{2\beta}{N-1}LH, which vanishes exactly at H⋆​(β)H^{\star}(\beta). Let ar=‖(Q⊤​H0)r‖22a_{r}=\|(Q^{\top}H_{0})_{r}\|_{2}^{2}. Since q1q_{1} is constant and λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0,

ρmc=AA+B,A=∑r=m+1Nar(1+τ​λr)2,B=∑r=2mar(1+τ​λr)2.\rho^{c}_{m}=\frac{A}{A+B},\qquad A=\sum_{r=m+1}^{N}\frac{a_{r}}{(1+\tau\lambda_{r})^{2}},\qquad B=\sum_{r=2}^{m}\frac{a_{r}}{(1+\tau\lambda_{r})^{2}}.

Each nonzero term satisfies dd​τ​log⁡ar(1+τ​λr)2=−2​φ​(λr)\frac{d}{d\tau}\log\frac{a_{r}}{(1+\tau\lambda_{r})^{2}}=-2\varphi(\lambda_{r}) with φ⁡(λ)=λ/(1+τ​λ)\varphi(\lambda)=\lambda/(1+\tau\lambda), which is increasing in λ\lambda. The path-Laplacian eigenvalues λr=4​sin2⁡((r−1)​π/(2​N))\lambda_{r}=4\sin^{2}\bigl((r-1)\pi/(2N)\bigr) are distinct, so λm+1>λm\lambda_{m+1}>\lambda_{m}, and A/BA/B, hence ρmc\rho^{c}_{m}, strictly decreases in τ\tau, which is proportional to β\beta. If A=0A=0 or B=0B=0, ρmc\rho^{c}_{m} is constant. ∎

The model inherits the limits of Appendix C.1. It ignores causality, since (I+τ​L)−1(I+\tau L)^{-1} mixes later positions into earlier ones, and its quadratic term charges for uniform rescaling, which rules out the scale route by assumption. With a feature-dependent curvature 12​Tr⁡((H−H0)​W​(H−H0)⊤)\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((H-H_{0})W(H-H_{0})^{\top}\bigr), W≻0W\succ 0, the conclusion holds within each eigendirection of WW but can fail for the total share. Whether the centered residual share of a trained model falls with β\beta is therefore an empirical question.

In a pre-LN Transformer the residual stream is not read only through normalization, so the invariance is approximate and we use the measured ratio ρl\rho_{l} (Table 21). Adam’s update is unchanged when the total loss is multiplied by a constant, and to first order in β\beta the CC term changes each coordinate’s update in proportion to β\beta times its CC gradient over the scale of its NTP gradient, which is why κl=β​ρl\kappa_{l}=\beta\rho_{l} is the natural strength.

Across gpt2-medium layers 10–20, ρl\rho_{l} grows 3.1×3.1\times and β⋆\beta^{\star} falls 2.2×2.2\times, so β⋆​ρl\beta^{\star}\rho_{l} stays within [0.0034,0.0059][0.0034,0.0059]. Its geometric mean predicts the best β\beta at medium layer 22 and small layer 10 to within 15%15\% of the three-seed vertices, and at medium layers ≤8\leq 8 it places the optimum just above the grid, where Table 3 has its best value. On gpt2-small the rule also holds at layers 2–8 except layer 4, which it misses by 2×2\times; there the three NLL values of Table 3 differ by at most 0.0120.012.

For CC, 𝖯\mathsf{P} is the path Laplacian acting on the representation, 𝖵\mathsf{V} the covariance of the representation’s estimation error, and g∗g_{*} the CC gradient at the population representation. The best weight is large when the estimation error is rough and the target trajectory is smooth, it decays like 1/n1/n, and the gain decays like 1/n21/n^{2} against an excess loss of order 1/n1/n. So CC’s relative benefit should shrink with the token budget, and the best β\beta should fall. Our runs agree in direction: CC adds about 0.3%0.3\% on top of BBC at 1B tokens but 0.06%0.06\% at 20B (0.14%0.14\% with adaptive dropout), and the 20B-horizon sweep selects a smaller β\beta. BBC’s gain does not shrink with training, so BBC does not act as a regularizer of this kind. The model gives the sign and the direction of the scaling, not the constants.

Appendix D Issues in the STP/LLM-JEPA Implementation

CC is partly inspired by the geometric prior on hidden-state trajectories introduced in (Huang et al., 2026b). While reproducing STP and LLM-JEPA results, we identified a subtle issue in the official implementation of both papers that affects the reported performance gains. The issue originates in the DataCollator used for training, which masks the labels of all padding tokens. For models whose EOS and PAD tokens share the same id, this also masks the EOS token itself, removing the training signal that teaches the model when to terminate the generation. Models with distinct EOS and PAD tokens are unaffected. We flagged this to the authors, who confirmed the issue and have since updated the implementation11 1 https://github.com/galilai-group/llm-jepa/commit/1c07b44fa2b0408a064be0ffc7816b5281384d7f.

After fixing the bug, we reproduced the results using Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the NL-RX-SYNTH dataset. NTP accuracy rose sharply, from 62.35% to 86.2%, while STP improved more modestly, from 84.35% to 86.31%. This gap suggests that STP is notably more robust to this failure mode than NTP. To probe this further, we ran a preliminary experiment masking the last two tokens. After one epoch, STP recovered to 72.55% accuracy, compared to 25.4% for NTP. This robustness did not extend to masking more than two tokens, however. Understanding why STP is able to partially recover from this kind of signal loss, while NTP is not, remains an interesting direction for future work.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
